description: Why schools exist: economy, social cohesion and mobility. Durkheim and Parsons versus Marxist critiques.
content_html:
What Is Education For?

Sociologists study education not just as a place where skills are taught, but as a social institution that shapes values, reproduces inequality and connects individuals to the wider society. Competing perspectives give very different answers to the question of what education is for — and whose interests it serves.

Key Fact

Functionalists argue that education performs three key functions for society: serving the needs of the economy, facilitating social mobility, and fostering social cohesion.

Durkheim: Transmission of Norms and Values

Functionalism begins from the assumption that social institutions exist because they serve a purpose. The French sociologist Émile Durkheim argued that education is the primary institution through which society transmits its values and norms to the next generation. Without this transmission, social solidarity — the glue that holds society together — would break down.

Durkheim identified two main functions of education. First, education creates social solidarity: by teaching a shared history, language and culture, schools turn individual children into citizens who feel they belong to the same community. Second, education teaches specialist skills that the economy needs — mathematics, literacy, technical knowledge — so that individuals can contribute to the division of labour in an industrialised society.

Parsons: Meritocracy and Achieved Status

American sociologist Talcott Parsons extended Durkheim’s analysis. Parsons argued that schools act as a “bridge” between the family and the wider society. In the family, a child is judged on particularistic standards — rules that apply only to that specific child, based on who they are. In wider society, however, people are judged on universalistic standards: the same rules apply to everyone, regardless of family background.

Parsons argued that schools prepare children for this shift by operating on meritocratic principles. In a meritocracy, exam results reflect genuine ability and effort. Students who work hard earn high grades and go on to high-status, well-paid jobs; those who do not earn lower grades and take less rewarding positions. The result is achieved status: people’s place in society reflects their own efforts, not their family background.

Students sometimes assume that a meritocracy means everyone ends up equal. It does not. Meritocracy means that unequal outcomes are fair because they reflect differences in effort and talent rather than background. Parsons’s point is that the inequality that results from a meritocracy is legitimate — it is earned. Critics from other perspectives challenge whether schools actually operate on meritocratic principles in practice.

The Marxist Critique: Education Serves Capitalism

Marxist sociologists challenge the functionalist view. From a Marxist perspective, education does not serve society as a whole but primarily serves the ruling class — the bourgeoisie. Rather than fostering genuine social cohesion, education reproduces the existing class hierarchy by disguising inequality as the result of individual merit.

Marxists argue that the “social solidarity” Durkheim describes is better understood as ideological control: schools teach working-class children to accept their subordinate position as natural and deserved. The hidden curriculum — the unwritten lessons about conformity, obedience and hierarchy — prepares working-class pupils for lives of routine employment. The claim that education facilitates social mobility is, for Marxists, largely a myth.

The Feminist Critique: A Gendered Institution

Feminist sociologists argue that the functionalist account ignores patriarchy. Historically, education was designed by and for men, preparing boys for paid work and public life while preparing girls for domestic roles. Even after formal barriers to entry were removed, feminists argue that schools continue to reproduce gender inequality through a gendered curriculum, teacher expectations and informal socialisation.

Functionalist: Education transmits shared values, creates social solidarity, teaches specialist skills and allocates roles meritocratically. Named theorists: Durkheim (social cohesion and specialist skills), Parsons (meritocracy and achieved status).

Marxist: Education reproduces class inequality, socialises workers into accepting exploitation, and presents ruling-class ideology as neutral common sense. The appearance of meritocracy legitimises an unequal system.

Feminist: Education reproduces gender inequality by channelling girls and boys into different subjects and career paths, reflecting and reinforcing a patriarchal society.

Interactionist: Rather than focusing on macro-level functions, interactionists examine how teacher expectations, labelling and pupil interactions shape individual outcomes within schools — a small-scale focus that functionalists and Marxists tend to overlook.

Key Fact

Parsons argued that schools bridge family and society by shifting children from particularistic standards (rules specific to the family) to universalistic standards (the same rules applied to everyone). This shift teaches children to compete on equal terms — the basis of a meritocracy.
exam_tip_html:
On a 12-mark Discuss question about education’s functions, students often give a one-sided functionalist account and forget to present contrasting perspectives. The mark scheme rewards candidates who present the functionalist view (Durkheim’s social solidarity, Parsons’s meritocracy), then challenge it using at least one other perspective (Marxist critique of ideological control, or feminist critique of the gendered curriculum), and reach a supported judgement. A strong conclusion weighs whether the evidence supports the claim that education truly serves all of society equally.

For 4-mark Describe questions, a common error is to describe only one function in vague terms. Aim for two developed points: name the function, name the sociologist associated with it, and describe the mechanism (e.g. “Durkheim argued that education creates social solidarity by teaching a shared history and culture, turning children into citizens with a common identity”).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Functionalists (Durkheim, Parsons) argue education serves society by transmitting norms and values, creating social solidarity, teaching specialist skills and allocating roles on meritocratic principles through achieved status.
  • Marxists challenge the meritocracy claim, arguing education reproduces class inequality and socialises working-class pupils into accepting their subordination through ideological control.
  • Feminists highlight the gendered nature of education, arguing that schools reproduce patriarchal inequality even when formal barriers are removed.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociologist argued that education creates social solidarity by transmitting shared norms and values?
A) Willis
B) Durkheim
C) Bowles and Gintis
D) Becker

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the principle of reward based on individual ability/effort; 1 mark for indicating that social position is earned rather than inherited or ascribed. Example: 'A meritocracy is a system in which social rewards (such as qualifications and jobs) are distributed on the basis of individual talent and effort, rather than family background or social class.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one function of education according to functionalist sociologists.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid function (e.g. serving the needs of the economy / fostering social cohesion / facilitating social mobility); 2 marks for a developed description that names a mechanism or sociologist. Example: 'Durkheim argued that education fosters social cohesion by teaching a shared history and culture, so that children from different backgrounds come to see themselves as members of the same society. Without this, social solidarity would break down.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Parsons's functionalist view of how schools prepare young people for adult society.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks for two developed points, each naming a relevant concept and explaining the mechanism. Points may include: (1) Parsons argued schools bridge family and society by shifting children from particularistic to universalistic standards — in the family a child is judged on who they are, but in school and society everyone is judged by the same rules. (2) Schools operate on meritocratic principles, so that students earn achieved status through their own effort and ability rather than inheriting their position. Links to a named theorist and clear explanation lift answers above 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way in which Marxists criticise the functionalist view of education.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid Marxist critique (e.g. education reproduces inequality / meritocracy is a myth / education transmits ruling-class ideology); 2 marks for a developed description explaining the mechanism. Example: 'Marxists argue that the claim of meritocracy is a myth: working-class pupils are disadvantaged by material deprivation and cultural capital, so exam results reflect social background rather than ability. Education therefore legitimises an unequal system by disguising class advantage as individual achievement.'

practice_questions.text: "Sociologists agree that education benefits all members of society equally." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Full range of relevant arguments for and against. Arguments for: functionalists (Durkheim on social solidarity and specialist skills; Parsons on meritocracy and achieved status) argue education does serve collective needs. Arguments against: Marxists argue education primarily serves the bourgeoisie by reproducing class inequality and passing off ruling-class ideology as neutral; feminists argue education reproduces patriarchy through a gendered curriculum and differential expectations. At least two perspectives developed with named sociologists. Sustained sociological vocabulary. A clear, supported judgement that weighs the evidence — e.g. concluding that while education may serve some collective functions, the evidence from class and gender inequalities in outcomes suggests it does not benefit all members equally. Secure (7-9): Most relevant arguments present, both sides covered, named sociologists referenced. Clear judgement though development may be uneven. Developing (4-6): Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion present but assertive rather than substantiated. Emerging (1-3): Basic description, few or no named sociologists, little or no judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: According to Durkheim, what is one key function of education?
options: Creating social solidarity by transmitting shared norms and values

knowledge_checks.q: Which term describes a social position earned through individual effort rather than inherited at birth?
Parsons argued that schools act as a bridge between the ______ and wider society by moving children from particularistic to universalistic standards.
Marxists argue that the appearance of meritocracy in education serves to ______ class inequality by making it appear the result of individual ability.
Match each sociologist to their key claim about education.
pairs: Education creates social solidarity by transmitting shared norms and values
Schools operate on meritocratic principles and prepare children for achieved status
Education reproduces class inequality through the correspondence principle
Counter-school cultures among working-class pupils challenge the meritocracy claim

flashcard_questions.q: What did Durkheim argue education does for society?
flashcard_questions.a: Creates social solidarity by transmitting shared norms and values to the next generation.

flashcard_questions.q: What are 'specialist skills' in Durkheim's view of education?
flashcard_questions.a: Subject-specific knowledge and abilities the economy needs from its workforce.
A social position earned through individual effort and ability, not inherited at birth.
A social position fixed at birth, such as family background or gender, regardless of effort.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Parsons mean by 'particularistic standards'?
flashcard_questions.a: Rules applied only to a specific individual, as in the family, based on who they are.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Parsons mean by 'universalistic standards'?
flashcard_questions.a: The same rules applied to everyone equally, regardless of background — as in schools and workplaces.

flashcard_questions.q: How do Marxists view the functionalist claim that education is meritocratic?
flashcard_questions.a: As a myth that disguises class advantage as individual achievement, legitimising inequality.

flashcard_questions.q: What is 'social cohesion' in the context of education?
flashcard_questions.a: A shared sense of belonging and common identity produced by learning the same culture and values.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the feminist critique of education's functions?
flashcard_questions.a: Education reproduces patriarchy by channelling girls and boys into different roles and subjects.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Parsons argue schools 'bridge' between?
flashcard_questions.a: The family (particularistic standards) and wider society (universalistic standards).

glossary_terms.definition: A sense of shared identity and belonging within a society, produced by common norms, values and culture.
A system in which social rewards are distributed on the basis of individual talent and effort rather than family background.
A social position that is earned through individual effort, ability or achievement, rather than inherited at birth.
Rules applied only to a specific individual within the family, based on personal relationships rather than universal principles.
Rules that apply equally to everyone in a society, regardless of personal background or family membership.
Movement between different positions in the social hierarchy, either upwards or downwards, across a person's lifetime.
A sociological perspective that views society as a system of interconnected parts, each performing a function that helps maintain social stability.
A social system in which men hold structural power and women are systematically disadvantaged across social institutions.

hero_image_caption: Schools are one of society's primary institutions — but sociologists disagree sharply about whose interests they serve.
